nodes.rationale: Marked as a contributed component. Automating mortality spotting replaces a manual walk-through inspection, so dead birds are removed sooner, which matters for both disease control and for keeping the recorded flock count accurate.

nodes.label: Chicken Weight Estimation
nodes.description: Second blue-shaded service in the callout-2 block: vision-based estimation of live bird weight.
nodes.rationale: Marked as a contributed component. Camera-based weighing avoids the sampling bias of platform scales, which only ever weigh the subset of birds willing to step on them, and it is non-contact so it does not disturb the flock.

nodes.label: Food Mix Optimization
nodes.description: Farm-management service that adjusts feed composition - the actuation-side consumer of growth and weight signals.

nodes.label: Data Storage Tier
nodes.description: Grey block holding two complementary stores: Blob storage for unstructured payloads (images, audio clips) and a SQL database for structured records.
nodes.rationale: Split storage keeps large media out of the relational store: blobs hold the raw evidence frames while SQL holds the queryable events and metrics that portals report on.

nodes.label: User Portal App Logic and APIs
nodes.description: Grey block containing user portal app logic, a web/mobile API app and a third-party API surface. It is the single presentation/integration boundary between platform services and all external consumers.
nodes.norm_label: user portal app logic and apis

nodes.label: Portals Swimlane
nodes.description: Rightmost dashed swimlane holding the three human-facing clients, each connected to the API layer by its own bidirectional arrow.

nodes.label: Command Center Portal

nodes.label: Mobile Inspection App

nodes.label: Admin Portal

nodes.label: El-Messery Broiler Thermal Imaging Sample Grid
nodes.description: Research figure: a 5-column x 4-row panel grid (rows labelled A1-A5, B1-B5, C1-C5, D1-D5) of paired thermal-infrared and RGB images of broiler chickens. Row A shows whole-bird IR thermograms with spot temperatures (36.8, 35.8, 36.5, 29.1, 31.9 C) and timestamps; row B shows the corresponding visible-light photographs with coloured bounding-box ROIs drawn over the bird/body region; row C shows cropped ROI thermograms annotated with Avg/High/Low temperature statistics (e.g. Avg 31 C, High 34 C, Low 25.8 C); row D shows segmented/thresholded false-colour temperature maps with the same statistics. Demonstrates an ROI-based thermal measurement pipeline: detect bird in RGB, register the box onto the thermogram, crop, then compute regional surface-temperature statistics.
nodes.rationale: Paired RGB+IR acquisition with a bounding-box ROI is used because a whole-frame thermogram includes floor, litter and background heat that biases the bird's true surface temperature; restricting statistics to a detected ROI isolates the animal and makes Avg/High/Low temperature comparable across birds and sessions.
nodes.norm_label: el-messery broiler thermal imaging sample grid

nodes.label: Thermal ROI Surface-Temperature Measurement
nodes.source_location: rows B-D of the panel grid
nodes.description: Method: draw a region of interest over the bird, crop the corresponding thermogram, and reduce it to Avg / High / Low temperature values plus a segmented false-colour map. Reported averages span roughly 29.6-39.8 C with highs to 40.9 C.
nodes.rationale: Scalar summary statistics per ROI make thermal state machine-comparable and enable thresholding for heat-stress classification without needing per-pixel calibration of the whole scene.

nodes.label: Broiler Surface Temperature Indicator
nodes.description: Body-surface temperature of broiler chickens measured non-invasively by infrared thermography and used as a physiological welfare / thermal-comfort indicator.
nodes.rationale: Surface temperature is preferred over cloacal or core temperature because it can be captured contactlessly at flock scale without handling stress that itself perturbs the measurement.

nodes.label: Heat Stress Effects on Poultry (Four-Quadrant Diagram)
nodes.description: Conceptual diagram: a sun radiating three curved yellow arrows onto a chicken at the centre, surrounded by four labelled quadrants that enumerate the consequences of heat stress - Behavioral Changes (top-left), Neuroendocrine changes (top-right), Physiological Changes (bottom-left) and Production changes (bottom-right). The sun-to-bird arrows encode the causal direction: thermal load drives all four response categories.
nodes.rationale: The radial layout is chosen to show that a single environmental stressor propagates simultaneously through behaviour, endocrinology, physiology and economic production outcomes rather than through one linear pathway.
nodes.norm_label: heat stress effects on poultry (four-quadrant diagram)

nodes.label: Heat Stress in Poultry
nodes.description: The central stressor of the figure: excess environmental thermal load on birds, depicted as solar radiation striking a chicken, which cascades into behavioral, neuroendocrine, physiological and production consequences.
nodes.rationale: Framed as the root cause node because every other category in the figure is drawn downstream of the radiation arrows.

nodes.label: Behavioral Changes Under Heat Stress
nodes.description: Spend less time feeding; more time drinking; panting; less moving or walking; wings elevated.
nodes.rationale: These are the only heat-stress responses that are externally visible, which is why they are the tractable target for camera-based automated monitoring rather than blood or hormone assays.

nodes.label: Neuroendocrine Changes Under Heat Stress
nodes.description: Increased corticotrophin releasing factor (CRF), adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH), catecholamines and plasma corticosterone; decreased T3, gonadotrophin releasing hormone (GnRH), FSH and LH.
nodes.rationale: Documents the HPA-axis mechanism linking perceived thermal load to suppressed reproduction and growth; requires invasive sampling, so it is background mechanism rather than a monitorable signal.

nodes.label: Physiological Changes Under Heat Stress
nodes.description: Oxidative stress; acid-base imbalance; respiratory alkalosis; increase in heterophil/lymphocyte (H/L) ratio; change in cecal microbial profile.
nodes.rationale: Respiratory alkalosis is presented as the direct consequence of panting, tying the behavioral quadrant mechanistically to the physiological quadrant.

nodes.label: Production Changes Under Heat Stress
nodes.description: Increased mortality; decreased feed intake; poor feed conversion ratio; reduced body weight; decreased meat quality; reduced quantity and quality of eggs.
nodes.rationale: Establishes the economic motivation for early heat-stress detection: the losses are realised in production terms, so an early behavioural warning has direct financial value.

nodes.label: Poultry Fecal Disease Data Collection App Screenshots
nodes.description: Three-panel figure documenting the collection protocol for a poultry fecal disease dataset. Left and right panels are mobile UI screenshots of an ODK/Android-style form titled 'Poultry Fec...' with a save icon and overflow menu; the left screen offers 'Take Picture' / 'Choose Image' buttons for a Fecal Image and a single-select 'Type of Image' radio group (Healthy, Coccidiosis, Newcastle, Salmonella, Other); the right screen continues the same radio group and adds a free-text 'Observations on Image' field and a 'GPS Reading' section with a 'Start GeoPoint' button. The centre panel is a field photograph of a data collector bending over to photograph droppings on a blue tarpaulin with free-range chickens around them.
nodes.rationale: Capture is done in-situ on a phone with a mandatory single-select label and an attached GPS geopoint so that each image is labelled at the moment of collection by the field worker rather than post-hoc, and so samples are geographically traceable for outbreak mapping.
nodes.norm_label: poultry fecal disease data collection app screenshots

nodes.label: Mobile Labelled-Capture Form Pattern
nodes.description: UI pattern: image acquisition control (camera or gallery) immediately followed by a constrained class picker, a free-text observation field and an automatic GPS reading, all in one saveable form.
nodes.rationale: A closed radio-button vocabulary prevents label drift across many field collectors, while the free-text field preserves nuance the fixed classes would otherwise discard; keeping label and image in one atomic record avoids the mismatch that arises when photos and spreadsheets are reconciled later.

nodes.label: Poultry Disease Class Taxonomy (Healthy, Coccidiosis, Newcastle, Salmonella, Other)
nodes.description: The five-way label set applied to each fecal image: Healthy, Coccidiosis, Newcastle, Salmonella, Other.
nodes.rationale: An explicit 'Other' bucket is included so collectors are never forced to mislabel an unfamiliar presentation into one of the four known classes.
nodes.norm_label: poultry disease class taxonomy (healthy, coccidiosis, newcastle, salmonella, other)

nodes.label: Raspberry Pi Single-Board Computer
nodes.description: Product photograph of a green Raspberry Pi board (Model B era, 2014 silkscreen, Samsung LPDDR SDRAM package, raspberry logo) on a plain light background, shot at an angle. Visible interfaces: a 40-pin GPIO header along the top-left edge, two stacked dual USB-A ports and an EDAC Ethernet RJ45 jack at the right, HDMI out and a 3.5 mm AV jack along the front, micro-USB power input, plus CSI camera and DSI display ribbon connectors and four mounting holes.
nodes.rationale: Used as the edge compute platform illustration: the 40-pin GPIO header supplies the digital I/O needed for environmental sensors and the CSI connector accepts a camera module, so a single low-cost board can host both sensing and on-device inference without a separate microcontroller.

nodes.label: 40-Pin GPIO Header
nodes.description: The general-purpose input/output pin header on the Raspberry Pi, providing 3.3 V and 5 V power rails, ground and single-wire digital data lines used to attach sensor modules.
nodes.rationale: Its VCC/GND/DATA pin availability is precisely what lets a one-wire sensor module be attached directly, with no ADC or level-shifting hardware in between.

nodes.label: Edge Compute Platform
nodes.description: Design choice of running sensing, data logging and model inference on a low-cost single-board computer deployed inside the poultry house.
nodes.rationale: On-site computation avoids dependence on continuous rural network connectivity and reduces the bandwidth and latency cost of streaming video off-farm; a general-purpose Linux SBC also allows the same device to run the detection model and read the sensors.

nodes.label: YOLO Unified Detection Pipeline Figure
nodes.description: The canonical YOLO 'The Model' schematic (dog-bicycle-car scene). A left panel shows the input image overlaid with an S x S grid; two outlined arrows fan out to an upper panel of many candidate 'Bounding boxes + confidence' with line thickness proportional to confidence and a lower panel showing a coloured per-cell 'Class probability map'; both streams converge through arrows into a right panel of 'Final detections' with three clean coloured boxes around the dog, bicycle and car.
nodes.rationale: The two parallel branches merging into one output is the whole argument of the figure: box regression and class prediction are produced by a single network pass over a grid, so detection becomes one regression problem rather than a proposal-then-classify cascade.

nodes.label: S x S Grid Division of Input
nodes.description: The input image is partitioned into an S x S grid; each cell is responsible for predicting boxes and class probabilities for objects whose centre falls in that cell.
nodes.rationale: Assigning responsibility by object centre gives each ground-truth object exactly one predictor, which keeps the loss well-posed and removes the need for external region proposals.
nodes.norm_label: s x s grid division of input

nodes.label: Bounding Boxes and Confidence Prediction
nodes.description: Per-cell regression of candidate box coordinates together with an objectness confidence score, drawn in the figure as box outline thickness.
nodes.rationale: Encoding confidence as a continuous score lets low-scoring boxes be pruned by thresholding and non-max suppression instead of by a learned second stage.

nodes.label: Class Probability Map
nodes.description: A per-grid-cell conditional class probability map, rendered as a coloured mosaic over the scene, predicted in the same forward pass as the boxes.
nodes.rationale: Predicting class per cell rather than per box keeps the output tensor small and fixed-size, which is what makes the single-pass real-time throughput possible.

nodes.label: Single-Stage Real-Time Object Detection
nodes.description: The design principle demonstrated by the figure: frame detection as a single regression from image pixels to boxes and class probabilities, evaluated in one network pass.
nodes.rationale: Chosen over two-stage detectors because one pass over the whole image gives global context and frame-rate inference suitable for constrained or embedded deployment; the trade-off is coarser localisation of small and clustered objects, which the fixed grid limits.

nodes.label: DHT22 / AM2302 Temperature and Humidity Sensor Module
nodes.description: Close-up photograph of a red breakout PCB silkscreened 'AM2302 DHT22 Sensor' carrying a white slotted plastic sensor housing marked 'AOSONG AM2302 SN17023IEEC'. A right-angle 3-pin male header exits the right edge, with the pads labelled DAT, VCC and GND on the silkscreen; two mounting holes and a pull-up resistor pad are visible. This is the actual hardware component used in the build, photographed as equipment documentation.
nodes.rationale: The 3-pin DAT/VCC/GND breakout is preferred over the bare 4-pin sensor because the pull-up resistor is already populated on the board, so it wires straight to a single-board-computer GPIO header with three jumper wires and no extra components.
nodes.norm_label: dht22 / am2302 temperature and humidity sensor module

nodes.label: Single-Wire DAT/VCC/GND Digital Interface
nodes.description: The module's electrical contract: power, ground and a single bidirectional data line carrying a digital temperature and relative-humidity reading.
nodes.rationale: A digital single-wire protocol removes the need for analogue-to-digital conversion, which matters because the Raspberry Pi has no on-board ADC.

nodes.label: Ambient Temperature and Humidity Monitoring
nodes.description: Continuous measurement of poultry-house air temperature and relative humidity as the environmental context signal for welfare assessment.
nodes.rationale: Humidity is measured alongside temperature because evaporative cooling by panting fails at high relative humidity, so temperature alone under-states the true thermal load on the birds.

nodes.label: MQ-135 Gas Sensor Module
nodes.description: Product photograph of a purple breakout PCB carrying an MQ-135 metal-oxide semiconductor gas sensor. The dome-shaped stainless steel mesh cap covers the internal heater and SnO2 sensing element; the mesh acts as a flame arrestor and diffusion barrier. Board is silkscreened 'MQx' with a Sensor-brand wave logo.
nodes.rationale: The MQ-135 is chosen for air-quality/ammonia and CO2-equivalent gas sensing in a poultry/livestock or environmental monitoring rig because it is low cost, 5V-powered, and exposes both an analog concentration output and a comparator-thresholded digital alarm, letting a controller act on gas levels without ADC calibration if needed.

nodes.label: LM393 Dual Comparator (on-board threshold circuit)
nodes.description: SOIC-8 chip marked 'LM393 IDCAB29' mounted on the MQ-135 breakout. It compares the sensor's analog voltage against a reference set by the on-board trim potentiometer and drives the DO digital output plus its indicator LED.

nodes.label: Sensitivity Adjust Potentiometer
nodes.description: Blue/silver multi-turn trimmer silkscreened 'ADJUST' that sets the comparator reference voltage, i.e. the gas concentration threshold at which DO trips.
nodes.rationale: Provides field-tunable trip point so the same board can be calibrated to a target ammonia/CO2 threshold for the enclosure without changing firmware.

nodes.label: MQ-135 4-Pin Interface (5V, DO, AO, GND)
nodes.description: Four labelled header pads on the board edge: 5V, DO (digital comparator output), AO (raw analog sensor voltage), GND. AO requires an external ADC when interfaced to a board with no analog inputs.
nodes.rationale: Exposing both AO and DO lets the designer trade off continuous concentration readings (needs ADC) against a simple binary threshold event (no ADC), which matters on a Raspberry Pi that has no on-board analog input.

nodes.label: Raspberry Pi 4 Model B Single-Board Computer
nodes.description: Top-down photograph of a green Raspberry Pi 4 Model B PCB (silkscreen 'Raspberry Pi 4 Model B, (c) Raspberry Pi 2018', FCC ID 2ABCB-RPI4B, Made in the UK). Visible: Broadcom SoC under a metal lid, LPDDR4 SDRAM package, 40-pin GPIO header (J8), gigabit Ethernet jack, 2x USB 3.0 and 2x USB 2.0 stacks, USB-C power in, dual micro-HDMI (HDMI0/HDMI1), CSI camera connector (J3), DSI display connector (J4), 3.5mm A/V jack, PoE header (J14), RUN/GLOBAL_EN test points.
nodes.rationale: Selected as the edge controller because it combines enough CPU/RAM to run computer-vision inference locally with the GPIO, USB and camera I/O needed to drive relays and read sensors on one board, avoiding a separate microcontroller.
nodes.norm_label: raspberry pi 4 model b single-board computer

nodes.label: 40-Pin GPIO Header (J8)
nodes.description: Double-row 2x20 male header along the top edge, silkscreened 'GPIO' / 'J8'. Provides 3.3V/5V rails, ground, and digital I/O lines used to drive actuator control signals and to read digital sensor outputs.

nodes.label: USB Host Ports (USB 3.0 J12 / USB 2.0 J11)
nodes.description: Two stacked dual-port USB blocks on the right edge: blue-tongue USB 3.0 (J12) and black USB 2.0 (J11). These are the attachment point for a UVC webcam used as the imaging input.
nodes.norm_label: usb host ports (usb 3.0 j12 / usb 2.0 j11)

nodes.label: CSI Camera Connector (J3)
nodes.description: 15-way FFC ribbon connector silkscreened 'CAMERA' / 'J3' for the native MIPI CSI-2 camera module — the alternative imaging path to a USB webcam.
nodes.rationale: Offers a lower-latency, non-USB imaging route; choosing USB webcam over CSI trades ribbon-length and driver simplicity against CSI's dedicated bandwidth.

nodes.label: USB HD Webcam (Microsoft LifeCam-style)
nodes.description: Close-up photograph of a black cylindrical Microsoft-branded HD USB webcam clipped to the top bezel of a laptop/monitor. Visible: 'HD' marking above the lens, a fixed glass lens in a ribbed barrel, a blue activity/status LED below the lens, a hinged tilt joint, and a rubberised monitor clip embossed 'Microsoft'.
nodes.rationale: A UVC-class USB webcam is used as the image capture device because it is plug-and-play on Linux (no driver work), mounts flexibly on an enclosure wall via its clip/tilt hinge, and can be placed away from the board unlike a short CSI ribbon.

nodes.label: Vision Image Capture Input
nodes.description: The role the webcam plays in the system: it is the sensing front-end that produces the image frames consumed by the on-device computer-vision/classification pipeline, complementing the non-visual gas/environment sensors.
nodes.rationale: Visual inspection captures conditions (appearance, behaviour, physical state) that chemical and thermal sensors cannot express, so the design pairs an imaging modality with scalar sensors for a fuller state estimate.

nodes.label: 2-Channel 5V Relay Module
nodes.description: Annotated callout diagram (labelled product photo) of a blue/black 2-channel relay board. Two blue Songle SRD-05VDC-SL-C relays rated 10A 250VAC / 10A 125VAC / 10A 30VDC / 10A 28VDC sit over two screw terminal blocks. Labelled parts: NO/COM/NC contacts per channel, control header GND/IN1/IN2/VCC, a second GND/VCC/JD-VCC header, a power-select jumper, and per-channel relay switch indicator LEDs.
nodes.rationale: A relay module is used so that low-voltage 3.3V/5V logic from the controller can switch mains-voltage actuators safely; the two channels give independent control of two distinct actuators from one board.

nodes.label: Optocoupler Isolation and JD-VCC Power-Select Jumper
nodes.description: The board carries per-channel optoisolators between the IN pins and the relay coil drivers, plus a 'power select jumper' bridging VCC and JD-VCC. Removing the jumper separates the logic supply (VCC) from the relay coil supply (JD-VCC).
nodes.rationale: Galvanically separating coil current from the controller's 5V rail prevents relay switching transients and inrush from browning out or resetting the single-board computer, which is the classic failure mode when driving inductive mains loads from a Pi.
nodes.norm_label: optocoupler isolation and jd-vcc power-select jumper

nodes.label: NO / COM / NC Contact Scheme
nodes.description: Each channel exposes a normally-open, common and normally-closed screw terminal, so a load can be wired to be either energised-on-command or energised-by-default and interrupted on command.
nodes.rationale: Wiring choice encodes the fail-safe behaviour: a load on NO defaults to OFF if the controller dies, a load on NC defaults to ON — critical when deciding whether ventilation or heating should persist during a controller failure.

nodes.label: IN1 / IN2 Active-Low Control Inputs
nodes.description: Two logic-level control lines on the GND/IN1/IN2/VCC header. Each drives one relay channel and its indicator LED. Modules of this family are conventionally active-low (pull IN low to energise the coil).
nodes.rationale: Active-low convention is noted because inverted control polarity is a common integration bug: a GPIO that boots low would energise the relay before software starts.

nodes.label: Wall-Mounted Ventilation Exhaust Fan (KDK)
nodes.description: In-situ photograph of a white square louvred wall/window exhaust fan (red KDK badge) mounted on a dark panel set into a tiled opening, with a white mains cable running up from the top of the unit. The louvre blades show visible dust and grime staining, indicating an in-service, non-laboratory installation.
nodes.rationale: An off-the-shelf mains exhaust fan is used as the ventilation actuator: it moves enough air to actually change enclosure gas concentration and temperature, and being a mains appliance it is switched through the relay rather than driven directly.

nodes.label: Ventilation Actuation (Air Exchange Control)
nodes.description: The control action of expelling stale air from the enclosure to reduce accumulated gas concentration and shed heat. It is the corrective response paired with a gas-concentration or temperature measurement.
nodes.rationale: Ventilation is the natural counter-actuator to gas build-up: it directly reduces the quantity the MQ-135 measures, closing a sense-decide-act loop on air quality.

nodes.label: Ceramic Infrared Heat Emitter Lamp
nodes.description: Studio photograph on black of a white ceramic infrared heat emitter with an E27 screw base. The emitting face is a flat disc with a moulded concentric spiral/labyrinth relief that follows the embedded resistive heating element and maximises radiating surface area. Emits infrared heat with no visible light.
nodes.rationale: A ceramic IR emitter is preferred over an incandescent brooder bulb because it delivers radiant heat without emitting visible light, so the thermal environment can be regulated without disturbing the day/night light cycle of the occupants — and, for a vision-based system, without corrupting the camera's illumination conditions.

nodes.label: Thermal Actuation (Radiant Heating Control)
nodes.description: The control action of raising enclosure temperature by radiant infrared output, switched on demand to hold a temperature setpoint.
nodes.rationale: Radiant rather than convective heating is used so heat reaches occupants directly and is not immediately carried away by the ventilation airflow, letting heating and ventilation be regulated semi-independently.

nodes.label: Low-Voltage-to-Mains Load Switching Pattern
nodes.description: Architectural pattern in which a 3.3V/5V GPIO signal from the controller drives an optoisolated relay coil, whose 10A/250VAC dry contacts carry the mains circuit of a household appliance.
nodes.rationale: Keeps all mains wiring off the computing board entirely; the only coupling is an optical one, so a fault on the load side cannot propagate into the controller, and the appliance needs no modification.

nodes.label: Batches List Screen (PMS Web UI)

nodes.label: Batch Record DEMO-B1
nodes.rationale: A single active batch row: code DEMO-B1, farm GreenFarms Demo Yaounde, status Active, age 53 days, current population 932, mortality 1.8%. The row exposes exactly the columns needed to triage a flock (identity, ownership, lifecycle stage, headcount, loss rate) and defers everything else to a 'View' detail action.

nodes.label: Batch Status Filter and Code Search Toolbar
nodes.rationale: Toolbar pairs an 'All statuses' select with a free-text 'Code...' box and a Go button. Server-side filter+search rather than client-side table sorting, which keeps the page usable when batch counts grow beyond one screen.

nodes.label: Mortality Percentage Column
nodes.rationale: Mortality % is surfaced as a first-class list column (1.8 for DEMO-B1), making flock loss the primary at-a-glance health KPI in the batch roster.

nodes.label: List-Toolbar-Table CRUD Layout Pattern
nodes.rationale: Every domain list page in the PMS web app reuses one template: H1 page heading on the left, filter/search controls plus a dark-green primary 'Add X' button on the right, then a full-width table with a pale-green header band and a right-aligned row action. Consistency lowers training cost for farm staff and lets new entity types be added without new interaction design.

nodes.label: Environmental Monitoring Screen
nodes.rationale: Screenshot of the 'Environmental monitoring' page: a chart panel on top, a long 'Latest readings' table beneath it, pagination, and a warning callout at the bottom. Chart-above-detail-table layout lets a user spot a trend and then inspect the exact rows behind it on the same screen.

nodes.label: Temperature Time-Series Chart
nodes.rationale: Line chart plotting the selected metric (temperature) over time with a legend swatch. In this capture the plot area is empty and the y-axis auto-scales to 0-1.0, i.e. the chart rendered with no series data even though the table below is full of readings - an apparent metric/series binding or aggregation-window mismatch worth flagging.

nodes.label: Latest Sensor Readings Table
nodes.rationale: Hourly rows (June 25-27 2026) with columns Time, Device, Temp, Humidity, Gas risk, Quality. Temperature spans roughly 23-31 C and humidity roughly 49-72%, consistent with a tropical Yaounde broiler house sampled once per hour.

nodes.label: Gas-Risk Index (Relative Ammonia Indicator)
nodes.rationale: Explicit footer disclaimer: 'Gas readings are a relative ammonia-risk indicator, not a calibrated ppm measurement.' Design intent is honest instrumentation - a cheap uncalibrated MQ-series gas sensor is reported as a normalised 0-1 risk score with a '(high)' qualifier above threshold, rather than being dressed up as a scientific ppm value the hardware cannot deliver.

nodes.label: Reading Quality Flag
nodes.rationale: Each reading carries a quality label ('good') so downstream aggregates can exclude suspect samples; the dashboard's 24h average explicitly reports how many good-quality readings it was based on.

nodes.label: Edge Device DEMO-PI-001
nodes.rationale: Single Raspberry-Pi-class sensor node identified as DEMO-PI-001 that authors every environmental reading in the table; naming implies a per-device provisioning scheme for the IoT tier.

nodes.label: Device and Metric Selector
nodes.rationale: Two dropdowns ('All devices', 'Temperature') scope the chart and table together, so one page serves temperature, humidity and gas-risk views instead of three separate screens.

nodes.label: Readings Pagination Control
nodes.rationale: Previous / 'Page 1 of 2' / Next control caps the readings table at ~30 rows per page, bounding query cost on high-frequency time-series data.

nodes.label: Farm Overview Dashboard Screen
nodes.rationale: Landing screen of the Poultry Monitoring System. Composition is an 8-tile KPI grid across the top, then a two-column body: wider left column for environment and alerts, narrower right rail for finance, vision predictions and inventory. Answers 'is anything wrong right now?' before offering any navigation.

nodes.label: KPI Tile Grid
nodes.rationale: Eight uniform cards (Active batches 1, Current population 932, Mortality today 0, Mortality rate % 1.8, Feed today kg 0, Critical alerts 0, Devices online 0, Devices offline 1), each with an all-caps label, a large numeral and a muted outline icon. Operational, health, and hardware status are deliberately given equal visual weight.

nodes.label: Mortality Rate KPI
nodes.rationale: Cumulative mortality rate of 1.8% shown as a headline tile, mirroring the per-batch mortality column so the farm-level and batch-level numbers reconcile visibly.

nodes.label: Devices Online/Offline KPI
nodes.rationale: Devices online 0 / devices offline 1 makes IoT link health a first-class dashboard metric, so stale sensor data is attributable to a dead node rather than misread as a calm environment.

nodes.label: Environment 24h Average Panel
nodes.rationale: Three-up summary of temperature, humidity and gas-risk index rendered as em-dashes because it is 'Based on 0 good-quality readings'. Showing an explicit no-data state plus the sample count, instead of a zero or a stale value, is a deliberate trust decision.

nodes.label: Open Alerts Panel
nodes.rationale: Feed of severity-badged alerts with relative timestamps: 'High gas risk (High)', 'Visual indicator: open_beak_stress (58%)', 'Visual indicator: lethargic (62%)', all 3 weeks 4 days ago. Environmental threshold alerts and machine-vision alerts are unified in one stream so the operator has a single place to look.

nodes.label: Recent Vision Predictions Panel
nodes.rationale: Lists the latest CNN classifications with confidence scores (healthy 0.50, healthy 0.50, open_beak_stress 0.58, lethargic 0.62, healthy 0.91). Confidence is always displayed next to the label so a 0.50 near-coin-flip cannot be mistaken for a diagnosis; only the higher-confidence abnormal classes were promoted into Open alerts.

nodes.label: Machine-Vision Advisory Disclaimer
nodes.rationale: Persistent footer callout: 'Machine-vision predictions are early-warning indicators and do not replace veterinary diagnosis.' Positions the ML tier as decision support, bounding liability and setting user expectations about model reliability - the same honesty principle applied to the uncalibrated gas sensor.

nodes.label: Inventory Warnings Panel
nodes.rationale: Low-stock watcher that renders a reassuring empty state (check mark, 'Stock levels OK.') rather than a blank card, confirming the check ran.

nodes.label: This Month Sales and Expenses Panel
nodes.rationale: Month-to-date roll-up of confirmed sales and expenses on the dashboard rail, linking the finance module into the operational overview.
nodes.norm_label: this month sales and expenses panel

nodes.label: PMS Grouped Sidebar Navigation
nodes.rationale: Fixed dark-green rail branded 'PMS', with items grouped under four all-caps section headers - Farm Operations (Farms, Pens, Batches, Mortality, Feed usage, Weights, Observations), Health (Health records, Treatments, Vaccinations), Inventory & Finance (Inventory, Expenses, Sales) and Monitoring (Devices, Environment, Vision review). The grouping is the information architecture of the whole system made visible, and the green palette carries the agricultural brand.

nodes.label: Signed-In User and Role Badge
nodes.rationale: Top bar shows 'Admin Demo' with a 'System Administrator' role chip, repeated as 'Signed in as Admin Demo (System Administrator)' on the dashboard. Persistent role display implies role-based access control where visible menu items and actions depend on the active role.

nodes.label: Expenses List Screen
nodes.rationale: Finance-module list page with Date / Category / Description / Amount columns, an 'All categories' filter and an 'Add expense' primary button - the same list template as Batches and Farms applied to a cost ledger.

nodes.label: Chick Purchase Expense Record
nodes.rationale: Single seeded entry: June 27 2026, category 'Chick purchase', description 'Day-old chicks (demo)', amount 500000.00 (XAF, unprefixed). Ties the batch lifecycle start to a capital outlay, enabling cost-per-bird analysis against the batch population of 932.

nodes.label: Expense Category Filter
nodes.rationale: Category dropdown implies a controlled vocabulary of expense types (chick purchase, feed, medication, labour) so spend can be aggregated by class rather than free-text description.

nodes.label: Farms List Screen
nodes.rationale: Top-level tenant/site registry page with Name / Code / City / Pens / Status columns, a search box and an 'Add farm' button. Farm sits at the root of the containment hierarchy farm -> pen -> batch, so this screen is the entry point for multi-site deployments.

nodes.label: Farm Record GreenFarms Demo Yaounde

nodes.label: Demo Data Badge

nodes.label: Add Feed Usage Form Screen

Narrow single-column layout keeps the form usable on a phone in a poultry house.

nodes.label: Feed Usage Record Fields
nodes.rationale: Fields are Batch*, Pen, Feed type*, Record date* (defaulted to today, 07/22/2026), Quantity kg* and Notes. Pen is optional while Batch is mandatory, so consumption is always attributable to a flock but only optionally to a physical location - matching farms where one batch spans several pens.

nodes.label: Required Field Marking Convention
nodes.rationale: Mandatory inputs carry a red asterisk beside the label and dates/numbers use native HTML5 date and number widgets, pushing basic validation to the browser and reducing round trips on low-bandwidth rural connections.

nodes.label: USB Webcam (Microsoft LifeCam HD)
nodes.description: Photograph of a black Microsoft-branded HD USB webcam with a cylindrical barrel body, glass lens behind a ribbed bezel, and a glowing blue status LED, clipped to the top bezel of a laptop/monitor. Serves as the vision input device of the poultry-house system.

nodes.label: HD Video Capture
nodes.description: High-definition video capture capability marked 'HD' on the camera bezel; provides the image stream used for visual inspection of birds.

nodes.label: Monitor Clip Mount
nodes.description: Hinged clip/foot on the underside of the camera that grips a display edge and lets the barrel tilt, allowing the camera to be aimed at a chosen field of view.

nodes.label: Visual Poultry Monitoring
nodes.rationale: A commodity USB webcam is chosen over an industrial/CSI camera because it is low cost, UVC class-compliant (driverless on Linux/Raspberry Pi), and its clip-and-tilt mount lets the field of view be re-aimed without re-engineering a bracket. Video adds a behavioural/visual channel that scalar environmental sensors cannot provide.

nodes.label: 2-Channel Relay Module
nodes.description: Annotated product diagram of a blue/black 2-channel 5V relay board. Callouts label the two Songle relays, NO/COM/NC screw terminals for each channel, the GND/IN1/IN2/VCC control header, a second GND/VCC/JD-VCC header with power-select jumper, and the two relay-switch indicator LEDs.

nodes.label: Songle SRD-05VDC-SL-C Relay
nodes.description: Two blue SONGLE SRD-05VDC-SL-C electromechanical relays, 5V DC coil, contacts rated 10A 250VAC / 10A 125VAC and 10A 30VDC / 10A 28VDC, CQC and UL marked.

nodes.label: NO / COM / NC Screw Terminals
nodes.description: Per-channel three-way screw terminal block exposing Normally Open, Common and Normally Closed contacts, letting a load be wired to energise either on or off.

nodes.label: IN1 / IN2 Control Inputs
nodes.description: Logic-level header pins GND, IN1, IN2, VCC that accept the controller's digital output signals; each IN line drives one relay channel.

nodes.label: JD-VCC Power Select Jumper
nodes.description: Jumper on the GND/VCC/JD-VCC header selecting whether the relay coil supply (JD-VCC) is bridged to the logic VCC or fed from a separate supply.

nodes.label: Optocoupler Isolation of Control and Coil Supply
nodes.rationale: The board routes each IN line through an optocoupler and separates JD-VCC (coil power) from VCC (logic power) so that inductive kickback and coil inrush from switching mains loads never travels back into the controller's GPIO. Removing the power-select jumper and feeding JD-VCC externally gives true galvanic isolation; leaving it fitted trades that isolation for single-supply wiring simplicity.
nodes.norm_label: optocoupler isolation of control and coil supply

nodes.label: Relay Switch Indicator LEDs
nodes.description: One LED per channel ('Relay switch 1/2 indicator') that lights when the corresponding relay is energised, giving at-a-glance confirmation of actuator state during commissioning and debugging.

nodes.label: Mains AC Load Switching
nodes.description: Switching of 230/250VAC mains loads at up to 10A through the relay contacts, which is what allows a 3.3V/5V logic controller to command grid-powered equipment.

nodes.label: Wall-Mounted Ventilation Fan
nodes.description: Photograph of a white square wall/window-mounted extractor fan (KDK-style) fitted into a dark panel, with a horizontally louvred front grille showing dust/soiling on the blades and a white supply cable running up out of frame.

nodes.label: Louvred Exhaust Grille
nodes.description: Horizontal-slat front grille that passes exhaust air while blocking large debris and birds; visible soiling on the louvres indicates the fouling/maintenance burden of an in-house fan.

nodes.label: Ventilation for Air-Quality and Humidity Control
nodes.rationale: An exhaust fan is the actuator that removes ammonia, CO2, dust and excess moisture from the poultry house. It is preferred to passive vents because it can be switched on demand from gas/humidity readings, but it also removes heat, so it must be arbitrated against the heat lamp rather than run independently.
nodes.norm_label: ventilation for air-quality and humidity control

nodes.label: Infrared Ceramic Heat Lamp
nodes.description: Studio photograph on black of a white ceramic infrared heat emitter bulb with a spiral/concentric ridged emitting face and a metal Edison screw base; radiates heat without visible light.

nodes.label: Ceramic Heat Emitter Element
nodes.description: Glazed ceramic face with an embedded resistive coil forming the concentric ridge pattern; converts electrical power to long-wave infrared radiation with no light output.

nodes.label: E27 Screw Base
nodes.description: Standard Edison screw cap allowing the emitter to be installed in ordinary mains lamp holders, so the heater can be switched by an in-line relay contact.

nodes.label: Brooding Temperature Control
nodes.rationale: A ceramic infrared emitter is chosen over a filament heat lamp because it produces radiant heat with no visible light, so the brooding set-point can be held overnight without disrupting the birds' photoperiod, and the ceramic body tolerates the dusty, humid poultry-house atmosphere.

nodes.label: Raspberry Pi Official 5V USB-C Power Supply
nodes.description: Product photograph of the official white Raspberry Pi AC adapter with US folding plug blades, regulatory/FC/UL markings on the body, a captive coiled white cable and a USB Type-C output connector.
nodes.norm_label: raspberry pi official 5v usb-c power supply

nodes.label: USB-C Power Connector
nodes.description: Captive USB Type-C plug terminating the adapter cable; matches the USB-C power inlet of the Raspberry Pi 4.

nodes.label: Regulated 5V DC Supply
nodes.description: Mains-to-5V DC regulated output (nominally 5.1V / 3A on the official Pi supply) that powers the controller and its 5V peripherals.

nodes.label: Poultry System Components Contact Sheet
nodes.description: A 2-column, 4-row captioned contact sheet tiling all eight system components with labels: DHT22 sensor, MQ135 gas sensor, Raspberry Pi 4, USB webcam, 2-channel relay, ventilation fan, infrared heat lamp, 5 V power supply. Functions as the visual bill of materials / figure plate for the build.

nodes.label: DHT22 Temperature and Humidity Sensor
nodes.description: AM2302/DHT22 module on a red breakout PCB with DAT, VCC and GND pins; supplies the temperature and relative-humidity readings for the house.

nodes.label: MQ135 Gas Sensor
nodes.description: Purple MQ135 breakout carrying a metal-mesh-capped gas-sensing element; detects ammonia, CO2 and other air-quality gases in the poultry house.

nodes.label: Raspberry Pi 4 Model B
nodes.description: Raspberry Pi 4 Model B single-board computer showing the 40-pin GPIO header, USB-C power inlet, dual micro-HDMI, USB 2.0/3.0 ports and Ethernet; acts as the system controller hosting sensors, camera and relay outputs.

nodes.label: Poultry House Environmental Monitoring and Control System
nodes.description: The overall system these components constitute: a Raspberry Pi controller reading temperature/humidity, gas and video, and driving a ventilation fan and infrared heat lamp through a 2-channel relay to hold the house microclimate at set-point.
nodes.rationale: The parts list is deliberately built from low-cost, widely available hobbyist modules (Pi 4, DHT22, MQ135, USB webcam, 5V relay board) so the system is reproducible and repairable in a smallholder poultry context rather than dependent on proprietary farm controllers.
nodes.norm_label: poultry house environmental monitoring and control system
